previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of gastroparesis, J-tube placement, and Nissen fundoplication was admitted for recurrent nausea, vomiting, and abdominal pain, consistent with her prior flares. She had been discharged three days earlier but developed symptoms suddenly after eating a small amount of jello. In the ED, she was found to have hypokalemia, which was corrected with IV potassium. She was treated with IV fluids, bowel rest, and IV antiemetics including ondansetron, lorazepam, and prochlorperazine, with good symptom control. Her pain resolved overnight, and she advanced to oral intake. Labs remained stable, with no signs of infection or organ dysfunction. She was discharged home with instructions to use her J-tube for feeds, try oral ondansetron (Zofran) for breakthrough nausea, and follow up with her gastroenterologist. Home health services were arranged for J-tube support.

Brief Hospital Course:
Ms. ___ is a ___ year old woman with history of gastroparesis 
s/p J tube placement, GERD s/p Nissen fundoplication, with 
multiple recent hospitalizations for nausea, vomiting, and 
abdominal pain, who presented again with similar symptoms.

# Nausea/vomiting/abdominal pain: Per patient, symptoms were 
consistent with her usual flares related to her gastroparesis. 
She has had multiple hospitalizations, most recently ___, 
and ___. Her longstanding recurrent symptoms began 
shortly after a ___ Fundoplication for GERD in ___. She is 
now s/p J tube though uses it intermittently. It remains unclear 
what is triggering her recent frequent flares; in the past, has 
been related to foods, but this present presentation seems to be 
related to the increased rate of her tube feeds. Prior work-up 
of her symptoms have been unremarkable. During this 
hospitalization, her abdominal exam was benign, and she was 
afebrile without leukocytosis. She received her usual set of 
meds: IV morphine, zofran, compazine, and ativan and her 
symptoms resolved by next day of admission. Her electrolytes 
were monitored closely and she was restarted on her home tube 
feeds which she tolerated well at target rate of 90 ml/hr. She 
had no further episodes of emesis and had resolution of her 
nausea during admission. Of note, she has had an extensive work 
up with Dr. ___ Dr ___ at ___ 
___ that has consisted of gastric emptying scan with 48% 
retained at 4 hours, esophageal manometry with reduced ___ 
___ pressure and normal ___. Also, she had 
severe, ineffective esophageal motility with only 1 of 10 
peristaltic swallows. Vagal nerve and mesenteric duplex testing 
were unremarkable. She has had trials of metoclopramide, 
erythromycin, domperidone, Zofran, Ativan, Compazine, 
bethanechol, and Phenergan suppository without any significant 
alteration in her symptoms. (please see ""outside records"" 
section of OMR for an excellent summary). Our gastroenterology 
team evaluated her during this hospitalization and with her 
extensive testing, noted that they had reached the limits of 
diagnostic and therapeutic interventions, recommending she 
continue her tube feeds with sips, and follow up with Dr ___ 
___ at ___ for further management of her symptoms.

# Metabolic acidosis: The patient presented with a metabolic 
acidosis, with bicarbonate to 17. This was thought to be most 
likely due to hypovolemia and emesis, similar to which she has 
had during previous admissions for nausea, vomiting, and 
abdominal pain. Her bicarbonate was monitored closely, and with 
IV fluids and her meds, improved to 22 at discharge. 

# Hypothyroidism: This was stable during this hospitalization, 
and patient was continued on her home levothyroxine dose.
